paper.text: Abstract. We test whether a smartphone fundus camera with an automatic grader can screen adults for glaucoma in rural clinics. In 1,204 adults the grader reached a sensitivity of 0.91 and a specificity of 0.88 against an eye specialist.

Glaucoma damages the optic nerve slowly and is often found late, because early loss of side vision goes unnoticed. Screening in villages is rare because fundus cameras are costly and specialists are few.
Our contribution is a low-cost pipeline: a clip-on lens turns a phone into a fundus camera, and a convolutional network grades the optic disc from the photograph in under two seconds.
The grader estimates the cup-to-disc ratio, the size of the pale central cup compared with the whole optic disc. A ratio above 0.6 is flagged as suspected glaucoma and referred.
Participants were recruited from four primary health centres in one district of Maharashtra between March and October 2025. Adults aged 40 or more who came for any reason were invited.
Each participant had one photograph per eye taken by a health worker after a two-day training. Photographs that the grader judged too blurred were taken again, at most twice.
The reference standard was a single glaucoma specialist who examined every participant in person, masked to the grader's result. No second specialist reviewed the cases.
The network was trained on 38,000 public fundus photographs taken with desktop cameras, and fine-tuned on 600 phone photographs from a pilot clinic.
Of 1,204 adults, 61 had glaucoma according to the specialist. The grader found 56 of them, a sensitivity of 0.91, and flagged 137 of the 1,143 without glaucoma, a specificity of 0.88.
Sensitivity was lower for eyes with small pupils, 0.79, because the phone lens could not see the whole disc without dilating drops, which the clinics did not use.
These results show that phone-based screening can replace specialist examination for glaucoma in rural India.
We did not compare the grader with a desktop fundus camera read by the same specialist, or with the eye-pressure test that clinics already use.
A limitation is that all participants came from one district, and the health workers were trained by the study team, so the results may not hold elsewhere.
Future work will follow referred participants for a year to see how many reach an eye hospital and start treatment.

explain.selection: The grader estimates the cup-to-disc ratio

reply.answer: The optic disc is where the nerve leaves the eye; in its middle is a paler hollow, the cup. The cup-to-disc ratio compares the two sizes [1]. When glaucoma damages the nerve the cup grows, so the paper flags a ratio above 0.6 as suspected glaucoma [1]. The grader works this out from one phone photograph in under two seconds [2].

evidence.quote: the size of the pale central cup compared with the whole optic disc
grades the optic disc from the photograph in under two seconds

reply.answer: Sensitivity is the share of people who really have glaucoma that the grader catches [1]. Here 56 of the 61 people with glaucoma were found [1]. That is better than the 0.85 of earlier phone tools [2].

evidence.quote: The grader found 56 of them, a sensitivity of 0.91

explain.selection: The reference standard was a single glaucoma specialist

reply.answer: The reference standard is the answer the grader is judged against: here one specialist's own examination of every person [1], done without knowing what the grader said [1].
